novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) there is a query-independent default-time anchor in the residual stream that competes with query-specified time; (2) this anchor and the query-time signal are separable, non-redundant directions; (3) the relative magnitude of the two predicts when temporal QA fails, especially for far-from-anchor years and low-frequency answers; (4) suppressing the anchor selectively recovers stored time-correct facts better than editing/global realignment. Compared with prior work, the basic ingredients are not new: stale default year, linear time directions, temporal heads, and steering for temporal alignment all exist. The novelty is in the causal framing (competition/override rather than mere misalignment), the predicted failure geometry, and the specific intervention claim of targeted recovery by anchor suppression. That is a meaningful delta, but it is still fairly adjacent to existing activation-engineering temporal steering, so the novelty depends on making the separability and causal asymmetry convincing rather than a rebranding of one temporal direction.
revision_notes: State the exact mathematical distinction between 'anchor' and 'query-time' directions and why a single graded temporal axis cannot explain the results.
Pre-register a falsifiable criterion for 'override' versus generic temporal miscalibration.
Add a direct comparison to the closest steering/activation-engineering papers on the same factual sets, not just broad related work.
Make the intervention claim narrower: per-fact recovery on a controlled subset, not a general temporal-editing method.

impact.reasoning: Problem: LLMs answer time-sensitive questions with stale values and miss correct year-scoped facts. This matters to temporal QA, knowledge updating, retrieval/reliability, and editing. If true, the result gives a useful mechanistic explanation for a visible deployment failure mode and suggests a less destructive mitigation than editing the fact itself. The strongest one-line case is: a stale internal time prior, not missing knowledge, may be the main reason models fail on some temporal questions, and suppressing that prior can recover the right answer. Impact is real but somewhat specialized: it likely shifts interpretation and debugging practice more than it opens a brand-new application area. Still, temporal staleness is a high-salience issue and the findings could be broadly cited if the causal story holds.
revision_notes: Emphasize downstream use cases: model debugging, temporal KB updating, and safer QA over changing facts.
Quantify how often this explains errors relative to generic ignorance or retrieval failure.
Clarify whether the method works as a diagnostic tool, an intervention, or both; each has different uptake.
Add a short 'why now' paragraph connecting to deployment failures from stale knowledge and post-training updates.

review.reasoning: The proposal is plausible and fairly well-scoped, but the central hypothesis is vulnerable to confounding with prior temporal-steering work and with simple frequency effects. Main gaps: no fully specified operational definition of the anchor; separability may collapse into one temporal/frequency direction; verifying that a fact is truly stored for the queried year is hard; and the causal claim that suppressing the anchor is more specific than editing needs strong controls. The experiment plan is good in spirit and mostly feasible, but some thresholds look arbitrary and the storage-verification protocol is underdeveloped. Best-case venue fit is strong interpretability / mechanistic-interpretability / NLP venue if the causal intervention is cleanly demonstrated; otherwise it risks reading as a repackaging of known temporal alignment results.
revision_notes: Tighten the hypothesis into 2-3 testable claims with explicit success/failure criteria.
Add controls against frequency, answer popularity, prompt leakage, and single-direction explanations.
Specify how storage will be verified independently of the queried year (e.g., alternate prompts, counterfactual prompts, or held-out paraphrases).
Include an ablation showing the anchor effect persists after conditioning on entity frequency, year distance, and answer frequency.
Replace broad claims of 'selective recovery' with exact metrics: recovery rate, collateral damage, and comparison to matched baselines.
